newsitem.title: UK: Adams to meet Irish premier on N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Adams to meet Irish premier on N.Ireland.

text.p: Prime Minister Bertie Ahern of Ireland will have talks with Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams on Friday, marking a growing acceptance of the IRA's political wing in the wake of the guerrillas' new ceasefire.
Officials said John Hume, leader of the moderate nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party in the British province of Northern Ireland, would also be present at the Dublin talks.

Following the Irish Republican Army's latest ceasefire, declared last weekend, Sinn Fein has been told that it can join peace talks on Northern Ireland in Belfast in September provided the truce is judged to be genuine.

Friday's Dublin meeting will mark the end of a 14-month embargo on meetings between the Sinn Fein leader and an Irish prime minister, imposed after the IRA broke its last ceasefire with a huge bomb in London in February 1996.
Ahern, who met Sinn Fein officials while he was in opposition, succeeded John Bruton after elections in June.
A parcel bomb sent to a Protestant politician in Northern Ireland on Thursday was packed with ball-bearings and could have killed whoever opened it.

The would-be Belfast attack highlighted the fragility of efforts to bring peace to the Protestant-majority province, scene of chronic sectarian conflict between pro-British Protestants and Roman Catholic republican nationalists.
The device sent to Robert McCartney, leader of the small pro-British UK Unionist Party, was "crude but viable", police said. It was made safe by army experts.
McCartney, who is on holiday abroad, told BBC radio: "The parcel, if opened, would probably have been fatal, or at the very least would have caused very disfiguring injuries."
McCartney said he had opposed the activities of both Irish republican and pro-British "loyalist" guerrillas and he was in the dark as to who might have sent the bomb.
McCartney, a member of the British parliament, added: "I think my defence of democracy has probably brought about this attempt.

"It's a matter of indifference which group this bomb can be sourced too, but the people who ought to be indicted for this are the British and Irish governments who have corrupted democratic politics in Northern Ireland by courting and wooing people who are wedded to terror."
The UK Unionists have walked out of the current round of peace talks on the future of Northern Ireland.
They and other unionist parties object to proposals to allow Sinn Fein into the talks without a commitment from the IRA to hand in their arms.
Adam Ingram, the Northern Ireland security minister, said the parcel bomb was a matter of regret although he did not think it represented a breach of the IRA ceasefire.

Some 3,200 people have been killed in the past three decades of conflict between Protestants and Roman Catholics in Northern Ireland. The IRA has waged a guerrilla campaign since 1969 to merge the province with Ireland.
The British and Irish governments are struggling to keep peace efforts on track after Protestant politicians on Wednesday rejected key proposals on the surrender of guerrilla arms.
The vote dashed hopes of a compromise on the surrender of guerrilla weapons after 14 months of deadlock and painstaking Anglo-Irish diplomacy.
